title: The Second Chance
author: Léxi
desc: À 42 ans, Rose, vendeuse de pagnes, décide de passer le bac en candidate libre — la même année que son fils. Une histoire sur le courage de recommencer.

p: Rose Gnahoré was forty-two years old when she found the envelope.

It was at the bottom of a cardboard box she was emptying after her mother's funeral, under old photographs and a rosary with three beads missing. Inside, carefully folded, was her report card from the final year of secondary school. 1999. *Première D, Lycée Classique d'Abidjan.* Mathematics: 16. Physics: 15. Philosophy: 14. And at the bottom, in the head teacher's neat handwriting: *Excellent student. Must continue her studies. A future doctor.*

She had never taken the baccalauréat. Three months before the exam, her father had lost his job at the port, and someone had to earn money. Rose was the eldest of six. She left school "for a year". She started selling pagnes at the Adjamé market with her aunt. Then she married. Then came the children, the rent, the school fees, the debts. The year became twenty-three years.
She sat on the floor of her mother's empty room and read the report card until the light faded.
That night, she told her husband she was going to sit the baccalauréat.
He laughed. Then he saw her face, and stopped.
The problem was not her husband. Bernard grumbled for two days and then, to her astonishment, bought her a calculator.
The problem was her son.

Junior was seventeen and in *Terminale D* — the very same class, the very same exam, the very same year. When Rose announced her plan at dinner, he put down his fork and stared at her with pure horror.
"Maman. You can't. Everyone will know. My friends will know. Imagine if you pass and I fail."
"Then you'd better study," said Rose calmly, and passed him the rice.

She registered as an independent candidate. She bought second-hand textbooks from a stall near the university, their margins already full of other people's notes. She studied before dawn, before opening her stall at the market, and late at night after the children were asleep. Some nights she fell asleep with her head on a chemistry book and woke up with the formula for glucose printed backwards on her cheek.

Mathematics came back to her almost immediately, like a language she had once spoken fluently. Physics was harder. Philosophy, which she had once loved, now terrified her: she had spent twenty years thinking about prices, not about Descartes.
Her stall at the market became an unusual place.
At first, the other sellers mocked her. "Professor Rose!" they called, when they saw her reading between customers. "Will you sell me a pagne with a little philosophy on top?"

But slowly, something changed. One morning, the young woman who sold shoes next to her — a girl of nineteen called Mireille, who had left school at fifteen — asked shyly what the book was about. Rose explained the chapter on probability using the pagnes: what are the chances that the next customer will choose the blue one?
The next day, Mireille brought her own exercise book.

A week later, there were four of them, sitting on upturned buckets behind the stall at lunchtime. A month later, eleven. Market women, a security guard, a young man who repaired phones. People who had all, for one reason or another, stopped studying too early. Rose taught them what she learned the night before. Teaching it, she found, was the best way to understand it.
The only person who never came was Junior. He avoided the market altogether, and at home he locked himself in his room with his headphones on.
Rose didn't push. But one night, very late, she heard a knock on her door.
"Maman," said Junior, staring at the floor. "I don't understand the thing about electric circuits. At all. Do you?"

The written exams took place in June, in a hot school hall in Treichville full of teenagers and their nervous energy. Rose was, by at least twenty years, the oldest person in the room. A boy in the next row asked politely if she was the supervisor.
"No," she said. "I'm your competition."

Her hands shook so much during the first exam, mathematics, that she couldn't read her own handwriting for the first ten minutes. Then something calm and old took over, the same steadiness that let her calculate a customer's change for fourteen items without a pen. She finished with forty minutes to spare.
Philosophy was the hardest. The subject was: *Is it ever too late to change your life?*

Rose stared at it for a long time. She thought it might be a joke. She thought about her mother's empty room, the report card, the upturned buckets behind the stall, Mireille's exercise book, her son knocking on her door at midnight.
Then she wrote eight pages without stopping, and for the first time in twenty-three years, she did not think about prices at all.
Junior was in another hall across the city. That evening, they compared their answers at the kitchen table, arguing loudly, until Bernard begged them both to go to bed.
The results were published on a hot morning in July, on long sheets of paper pinned to the gates of the examination centre, and on a website that crashed within five minutes.

Rose and Junior went together. They pushed through the crowd of shouting, crying, dancing teenagers. Junior found his name first: *Admis. Mention Assez Bien.* He screamed so loudly that a girl next to him dropped her phone.
Then he went quiet. He ran his finger down the list, looking for his mother's name. Rose couldn't look. She stood with her eyes closed, hearing her heart.
"Maman," said Junior, in a strange voice.
She opened her eyes.
*GNAHORÉ Rose Épouse YAO — Admise. Mention Bien.*
Better than her son. Junior looked at the list for a long moment. Then he burst out laughing and lifted her off the ground, in the middle of the crowd, while strangers cheered without knowing why.
In September, Rose started a degree in biology at the University of Cocody. She is the oldest student in her lecture hall, and the only one who brings homemade attiéké for the whole row.
Behind her stall at the Adjamé market, on Saturdays, the upturned buckets are still there. There are thirty of them now. Mireille, who passed her own exam the following year, runs the class.
